ja.title: 韓国語の語順（S-O-V）
ja.summary: 動詞は常に最後にあります。他はすべて柔軟です。助詞が意味を担うから。

sections.heading: 主語-目的語-動詞
sections.explanation: 英語はS-V-O：「I eat bread.」韓国語はS-O-V：「I bread eat.」動詞が最後に来ることに慣れると、ほとんどの文が乱雑に感じなくなります。

sections.heading: 助詞が機能を果たすので、順序は変わる可能性があります
sections.explanation: 은/는は主題をマークし、을/를は目的語をマークするため、強調するためにこれらのチャンクを移動できますが、文の意味は変わりません。動詞だけが末尾に固定されています。

sections.heading: 明白なことは省略できます
sections.explanation: 文脈が明確なときは常に、韓国語は主語を省略します。1語の回答は完全な文です。

quiz: 韓国語の文で動詞はどこに行きますか？
どの文が「私は韓国語を勉強します」を意味しますか？
韓国語がフレーズを自由に移動できるのはなぜですか？

zh.title: 韩语词序（主宾谓）
zh.summary: 动词总是放在最后。其他都很灵活，因为助词承载意思。

sections.heading: 主语–宾语–动词
sections.explanation: 英语是主语–动词–宾语："I eat bread。"韩语是主语–宾语–动词："I bread eat。"一旦你习惯了动词在末尾，大多数句子就不会显得混乱了。

sections.heading: 助词做功能，所以顺序可以变动
sections.explanation: 因为은/는标记主题，을/를标记宾语，你可以移动这些块来强调，句子的意思仍然相同。只有动词被固定在末尾。

sections.heading: 你可以省略明显的部分
sections.explanation: 当上下文清楚时，韩语会省略主语。一个词的回答就是完整句子。

quiz: 韩语句子中动词放在哪里？
哪个句子表示"我学韩语"？
为什么韩语可以这么自由地移动短语？

vi.title: Trật tự từ trong tiếng Hàn (S-O-V)
vi.summary: Động từ luôn đứng cuối. Phần còn lại linh hoạt vì các hạt từ mang ý nghĩa.

sections.heading: Chủ ngữ – Tân ngữ – Động từ
sections.explanation: Tiếng Anh là Chủ ngữ–Động từ–Tân ngữ: "I eat bread." Tiếng Hàn là Chủ ngữ–Tân ngữ–Động từ: "I bread eat." Khi bạn quen với động từ ở cuối, hầu hết câu sẽ không còn cảm giác lộn xộn.

sections.heading: Hạt từ thực hiện công việc, nên thứ tự có thể thay đổi
sections.explanation: Vì 은/는 đánh dấu chủ đề và 을/를 đánh dấu tân ngữ, bạn có thể di chuyển các khối này xung quanh để nhấn mạnh và câu vẫn có cùng ý nghĩa. Chỉ có động từ được khóa ở cuối.

sections.heading: Bạn có thể bỏ qua những gì hiển nhiên
sections.explanation: Tiếng Hàn bỏ qua chủ ngữ bất cứ khi nào bối cảnh rõ ràng. Một câu trả lời từ là một câu hoàn chỉnh.

quiz: Động từ đứng ở đâu trong câu tiếng Hàn?
Câu nào có nghĩa là "Tôi học tiếng Hàn"?
Tại sao tiếng Hàn có thể di chuyển cụm từ một cách tự do như vậy?

ja.title: 은/는 vs 이/가
ja.summary: 은/는はトピックを設定し、対比を招きます。이/가は誰がちょうど何かをしているかを指します。

sections.heading: 形式
sections.explanation: 子音の後は은と이を使用します。母音の後は는と가を使用します。これはあなたが必要な唯一のスペルルールです。

sections.heading: 은/는：「について…」
sections.explanation: 은/는は文が何についてかを発表し、静かに他と比較します。自分自身を紹介し、2つのことを対比するのに使用します。

sections.heading: 이/가：「これはこれです」
sections.explanation: 이/가は主語を識別します。特に新しい情報または「誰ですか？」と「何ですか？」の答えです。また、있어요/없어요および좋다のような記述的動詞に必要です。

quiz: 선생님のような子音で終わる単語の後に来る助詞はどれですか？
"誰が来ましたか？" — "친구___ 왔어요。"どれが合いますか？
あなたは対比したいのです：「私はコーヒーが好きですが、紅茶は好きではありません。」どの助詞が커피と차をマークしていますか？

zh.title: 은/는 vs 이/가
zh.summary: 은/는设置主题并邀请对比。이/가指出谁确切在做某事。

sections.heading: 形式
sections.explanation: 辅音后用은和이。元音后用는和가。这是你需要的唯一拼写规则。

sections.heading: 은/는："至于…"
sections.explanation: 은/는宣布句子讲的是什么，并隐含地与其他东西比较。用它介绍自己和对比两件事。

sections.heading: 이/가："就是这个"
sections.explanation: 이/가识别主语，特别是新信息或"谁？"和"什么？"的答案。它也需要与있어요/없어요以及좋다等描述词搭配。

quiz: 哪个助词跟在선생님这样以辅音结尾的词后面？
"谁来了？" — "친구___ 왔어요。"哪个适合？
你想对比："我喜欢咖啡，但茶不喜欢。"哪个助词标记커피和차？

vi.title: 은/는 vs 이/가
vi.summary: 은/는đặt chủ đề và mời so sánh. 이/가 chỉ ra chính xác ai đang làm điều gì.

sections.heading: Các hình thức
sections.explanation: Sau phụ âm dùng 은 và 이. Sau nguyên âm dùng 는 và 가. Đây là quy tắc chính tả duy nhất bạn cần.

sections.heading: 은/는: "Nói về…"
sections.explanation: 은/는công bố câu nói về cái gì và im lặng so sánh với cái khác. Dùng nó để giới thiệu bản thân và để tương phản hai điều.

sections.heading: 이/가: "Chính là cái này"
sections.explanation: 이/가 xác định chủ ngữ, đặc biệt là thông tin mới hoặc câu trả lời cho "ai?" và "cái gì?". Nó cũng cần thiết với 있어요/없어요 và với các động từ mô tả như 좋다.

quiz: Hạt từ nào đứng sau một từ kết thúc bằng phụ âm như 선생님?
"Ai đến rồi?" — "친구___ 왔어요." Cái nào phù hợp?
Bạn muốn tương phản: "Tôi thích cà phê, nhưng trà thì không." Hạt từ nào đánh dấu 커피 và 차?

ja.title: 目的語マーカー을/를
ja.summary: 을で作用を受けるもの（子音の後）、를で（母音の後）をマークします。

sections.heading: どちらを使うか
sections.explanation: 을は子音で終わる名詞の後に来ます。를は母音の後です。選択は純粋に音の問題です。

sections.heading: アクションの受信者に接着します
sections.explanation: 食べられる、見られる、買われる、または学ばれるものは何でも을/를がかかります。가다のような動作動詞は代わりに에を使用し、을/를ではありません。

sections.heading: カジュアルな会話では消えます
sections.explanation: スポークン韓国語は意味が明白な場合、常に을/를を削除します。書き言葉と丁寧な話し方で保ちます。

quiz: 책は子音で終わります。どの目的語マーカーがそれに続きますか？
"私はコーヒーを飲む"正しい文はどれですか？
을/를は何をマークしていますか？

zh.title: 宾语标记을/를
zh.summary: 用을标记被作用的东西（辅音后），用를（元音后）。

sections.heading: 使用哪一个
sections.explanation: 을跟在以辅音结尾的名词后；를跟在元音后。选择完全是声音问题。

sections.heading: 它附加到动作的接收者
sections.explanation: 无论吃什么、看什么、买什么或学什么都用을/를。动词가다等运动动词改用에，不用을/를。

sections.heading: 在日常语中消失
sections.explanation: 当意思明显时，口语韩语经常省略을/를。在书写和正式语中保留它。

quiz: 책以辅音结尾。哪个宾语标记跟在它后面？
"我喝咖啡"哪个句子正确？
을/를标记什么？

vi.title: Đánh dấu tân ngữ 을/를
vi.summary: Đánh dấu thứ bị tác động với 을 (sau phụ âm), 를 (sau nguyên âm).

sections.heading: Cái nào để dùng
sections.explanation: 을 đứng sau danh từ kết thúc bằng phụ âm; 를 đứng sau danh từ kết thúc bằng nguyên âm. Sự lựa chọn hoàn toàn về âm thanh.

sections.heading: Nó gắn với người nhận hành động
sections.explanation: Bất kỳ thứ gì được ăn, xem, mua hoặc học đều có 을/를. Động từ chuyển động như 가다 dùng 에 thay vì 을/를.

sections.heading: Trong nói chuyện hàng ngày nó biến mất
sections.explanation: Tiếng Hàn nói chuyện thường xuyên bỏ 을/를 khi ý nghĩa rõ ràng. Giữ nó trong viết và trong nói chuyện chuẩn mực.

quiz: 책 kết thúc bằng phụ âm. Hạt từ tân ngữ nào đứng sau nó?
Câu nào đúng cho "Tôi uống cà phê"?
을/를 đánh dấu cái gì?

ja.title: 이에요 / 예요 — 「です」
ja.summary: 名詞に이에요または예요を付けて「です/私は/あなたは」と言う。

sections.heading: 名詞 + 이에요/예요
sections.explanation: 子音の後は이에요、母音の後は예요を使用します。「です」という別の単語はありません—名詞に直接付きます。

sections.heading: 質問と否定
sections.explanation: 質問の場合は同じ形式を保ち、イントネーションを上げます。「ではない」の場合は이/가 아니에요を使用します。

sections.heading: 있어요と混同しないでください
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요は「XはYです」を意味します。있어요は「ある/私は持っている」を意味します。それらは交換可能ではありません。

quiz: 의사は母音で終わります。正しい形式はどれですか？
あなたは「私は学生ではありません」とどう言いますか？
どの文が「私は友人がいます」を意味しますか？

zh.title: 이에요 / 예요 — "是"
zh.summary: 在名词后加이에요或예요来说"是/我是/你是"。

sections.heading: 名词 + 이에요/예요
sections.explanation: 辅音后用이에요，元音后用예요。没有单独的"是"——它直接粘在名词上。

sections.heading: 问句和否定
sections.explanation: 问句时保持同样形式并提高语调。"不是"时用이/가아니에요。

sections.heading: 不要与있어요混淆
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요意思是"X是Y"。있어요意思是"有/存在"。它们不能互换。

quiz: 의사以元音结尾。哪个形式正确？
你怎么说"我不是学生"？
哪个表示"我有朋友"？

vi.title: 이에요 / 예요 — "là"
vi.summary: Gắn 이에요 hoặc 예요 vào danh từ để nói "là/tôi là/bạn là".

sections.heading: Danh từ + 이에요/예요
sections.explanation: Dùng 이에요 sau phụ âm và 예요 sau nguyên âm. Không có từ riêng biệt cho "là" — nó dính thẳng vào danh từ.

sections.heading: Câu hỏi và phủ định
sections.explanation: Để hỏi, giữ nguyên hình thức và nâng cao giọng. Để "không phải là", dùng 이/가 아니에요.

sections.heading: Đừng nhầm lẫn với 있어요
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요 có nghĩa là "X là Y". 있어요 có nghĩa là "có/tồn tại". Chúng không thể thay thế cho nhau.

quiz: 의사 kết thúc bằng nguyên âm. Hình thức nào đúng?
Bạn nói "Tôi không phải là học sinh" như thế nào?
Cái nào có nghĩa là "Tôi có một người bạn"?

ja.title: 現在時制 아요 / 어요
ja.summary: 辞書形式から다を削除し、最後の母音に応じて아요または어요を追加します。

sections.heading: ルール
sections.explanation: 動詞の幹を取ります（辞書形式から다を引く）。最後の母音がㅏまたはㅗの場合は아요を追加します。そうでなければ어요を追加します。하다動詞は不規則で해요になります。

sections.heading: 母音がマージされるとき
sections.explanation: ステムがすでにㅏまたはㅓで終わっている場合、아/어は2倍にされるのではなく吸収されます。오 + 아요は와요に縮約され、우 + 어요は워요に縮約されます。

sections.heading: 1つの形式、3つの仕事
sections.explanation: 아요/어요は現在、近い未来、および習慣的なアクションをカバーします。イントネーション だけで質問に変わります。

quiz: 먹다の現在時制形式は何ですか？
공부하다は…になります
どの語幹が아요を取りますか？

zh.title: 现在时 아요 / 어요
zh.summary: 从字典形去掉다，然后根据最后的元音加아요或어요。

sections.heading: 规则
sections.explanation: 取动词词干（字典形去掉다）。如果最后的元音是ㅏ或ㅗ，加아요。否则加어요。하다动词不规则，变成해요。

sections.heading: 当元音合并
sections.explanation: 如果词干已经以ㅏ或ㅓ结尾，아/어被吸收而不是加倍。오 + 아요缩为와요，우 + 어요缩为워요。

sections.heading: 一种形式，三个功能
sections.explanation: 아요/어요涵盖现在、近期未来和习惯性动作。只靠语调就能变成问句。

quiz: 먹다的现在时形式是什么？
공부하다变成…
哪些词干用아요？

vi.title: Thì hiện tại 아요 / 어요
vi.summary: Bỏ 다 từ hình thức từ điển, sau đó thêm 아요 hoặc 어요 tùy theo nguyên âm cuối cùng.

sections.heading: Quy tắc
sections.explanation: Lấy gốc động từ (hình thức từ điển trừ 다). Nếu nguyên âm cuối cùng của nó là ㅏ hoặc ㅗ, thêm 아요. Ngược lại thêm 어요. Động từ 하다 bất quy tắc và trở thành 해요.

sections.heading: Khi nguyên âm kết hợp
sections.explanation: Nếu gốc đã kết thúc bằng ㅏ hoặc ㅓ, thì 아/어 được hấp thụ chứ không phải được nhân đôi. ​​오 + 아요 co lại thành 와요, và 우 + 어요 thành 워요.

sections.heading: Một hình thức, ba công việc
sections.explanation: 아요/어요 bao gồm hiện tại, tương lai gần và hành động thường xuyên. Chỉ cần giọng nói là có thể biến nó thành câu hỏi.

quiz: Hình thức thì hiện tại của 먹다 là gì?
공부하다 trở thành…
Những gốc nào dùng 아요?

ja.title: 否定：안と지않다
ja.summary: 動詞の前に안を置いて素早く否定するか、語幹に지않아요を付けてより正式な否定にする。

sections.heading: 안 + 動詞
sections.explanation: 短い形式です。共役動詞の直前に안を置くだけです。これは会話で最も聞く形式です。

sections.heading: 語幹 + 지않아요
sections.explanation: 長い形式です。やや正式で、より強調され、書き言葉で一般的です。안と同じ意味です。

sections.heading: 하다動詞は分割します
sections.explanation: 하다の複合語については、안は名詞と하다の間に入ります—全体の前ではありません。また、있다の反対は別の単語없다であり、알다の反対は모르다です。

quiz: 공부해요をどのように否定しますか？
먹어요の長い否定形式はどれですか？
있어요の反対は何ですか？

zh.title: 否定：안和 지않다
zh.summary: 在动词前放안来快速否定，或在词干后附지않아요来更正式的否定。

sections.heading: 安 + 动词
sections.explanation: 简短形式。只在共轭动词前放안。这是你在会话中最常听到的。

sections.heading: 词干 + 지않아요
sections.explanation: 长形式。稍微更正式和更强调，在写作中常见。与안的意思相同。

sections.heading: 하다动词分裂
sections.explanation: 对于하다复合词，안在名词和하다之间——不在整个东西前面。还要注意있다的反义是单独的무없다，알다的是모르다。

quiz: 你怎么否定공부해요？
먹어요的长否定形式是哪个？
있어요的反义是什么？

vi.title: Phủ định: 안 và 지않다
vi.summary: Đặt 안 trước động từ để phủ định nhanh, hoặc gắn 지않아요 vào gốc để phủ định chính thức hơn.

sections.heading: 안 + động từ
sections.explanation: Hình thức ngắn. Chỉ cần đặt 안 ngay trước động từ chia. Đây là cách bạn sẽ nghe nhiều nhất trong cuộc trò chuyện.

sections.heading: Gốc + 지않아요
sections.explanation: Hình thức dài. Hơi chính thức hơn và nhấn mạnh hơn, phổ biến trong viết. Cùng ý nghĩa với 안.

sections.heading: Động từ 하다 tách rời
sections.explanation: Với các từ ghép 하다, 안 đi giữa danh từ và 하다 — không phải ở trước cả thứ. Cũng lưu ý rằng phản đối của 있다 là từ riêng 없다, và của 알다 là 모르다.

quiz: Bạn phủ định 공부해요 như thế nào?
Hình thức phủ định dài của 먹어요 là cái nào?
Phản đối của 있어요 là gì?

ja.title: 過去時制 았어요 / 었어요
ja.summary: 現在のように共役し、요をㅆ어요に交換します。

sections.heading: ショートカット
sections.explanation: 最初に아요/어요の形式を作成し、요を削除して、そのシラブルにㅆ어요を追加します。가요 → 갔어요。これはほぼすべての動詞に対して機能します。

sections.heading: 完全な文で
sections.explanation: 文の他に何も変わりません—動詞の終わりだけが過去に移動します。

sections.heading: 「です」の過去時制
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요は이었어요/였어요になり、있어요/없어요は있었어요/없었어요になります。

quiz: 가요の過去時制は何ですか？
해요の過去時制は…
"昨日友人に会いました"は…

zh.title: 过去时 았어요 / 었어요
zh.summary: 共轭成现在式，然后交换요为ㅆ어요。

sections.heading: 快捷方式
sections.explanation: 先做아요/어요形式，去掉요，加ㅆ어요。가요 → 갔어요。这对几乎每个动词都有用。

sections.heading: 在完整句子中
sections.explanation: 句子中没有其他东西改变——只有动词结尾移到过去时。

sections.heading: "是"的过去时
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요变成이었어요/였어요，있어요/없어요变成있었어요/없었어요。

quiz: 가요的过去时是什么？
해요的过去时是…
"我昨天见了朋友"是…

vi.title: Thì quá khứ 았어요 / 었어요
vi.summary: Chia như hiện tại, sau đó hoán đổi 요 thành ㅆ어요.

sections.heading: Phím tắt
sections.explanation: Làm hình thức 아요/어요 trước, bỏ 요, và thêm ㅆ어요 vào âm tiết đó. 가요 → 갔어요. Điều này hoạt động cho hầu hết mọi động từ.

sections.heading: Trong câu hoàn chỉnh
sections.explanation: Không có gì khác trong câu thay đổi — chỉ kết thúc động từ chuyển sang quá khứ.

sections.heading: Quá khứ của "là"
sections.explanation: 이에요/예요 trở thành 이었어요/였어요, và 있어요/없어요 trở thành 있었어요/없었어요.

quiz: Thì quá khứ của 가요 là gì?
해요 ở quá khứ là…
"Tôi gặp một người bạn hôm qua" là…

ja.title: 에と에서
ja.summary: 에は目的地または時点をマークします。에서はアクションが起こる場所をマークします。

sections.heading: 에——あなたが行く場所、それが起こるとき
sections.explanation: 移動動詞（가다、오다）および있다/없다を使用して、何かが座っている場所で使用します。また、時間と日付に付きます。

sections.heading: 에서——アクションが起こる場所
sections.explanation: 食べる、勉強する、働くなど、実際のアクティビティが起こる場所には에서を使用します。また、起点から「から」を意味します。

sections.heading: 1つのペアの対比
sections.explanation: "집에 있어요"は状態です—私は家にいます。"집에서 일해요"はアクションです—私は家で働きます。実際に何かがそこで行われているかどうかを自分に聞いてください。

quiz: 「私は学校で勉強します」は학교の後どの助詞を使いますか？
"私は学校に行きます"正しい文はどれですか？
「ある」以外に에서は何を意味しますか？

zh.title: 에和에서
zh.summary: 에标记目的地或时间点；에서标记动作发生的地方。

sections.heading: 에——你去的地方，它发生的时间
sections.explanation: 与运动动词（가다、오다）和있다/없다搭配使用表示东西坐在哪里。它也附加在时间和日期。

sections.heading: 에서——动作发生的地方
sections.explanation: 如果真实活动发生在某处——吃东西、学习、工作——用에서。它也意味着"从"一个起点。

sections.heading: 一对中的对比
sections.explanation: "집에있어요"是状态——我在家。"집에서일해요"是动作——我在家工作。问自己是否真的有东西在那里做。

quiz: "我在学校学习"在학교后面用哪个助词？
"我去上学"哪个正确？
除了"在"之外，에서还表示什么？

vi.title: 에 và 에서
vi.summary: 에 đánh dấu điểm đến hoặc thời gian; 에서 đánh dấu nơi hành động xảy ra.

sections.heading: 에 — nơi bạn đi, khi nó xảy ra
sections.explanation: Dùng 에 với động từ chuyển động (가다, 오다) và với 있다/없다 cho nơi thứ gì đó ở. Nó cũng gắn vào thời gian và ngày tháng.

sections.heading: 에서 — nơi hành động xảy ra
sections.explanation: Nếu hoạt động thực tế xảy ra ở đâu đó — ăn, học tập, làm việc — dùng 에서. Nó cũng có nghĩa là "từ" một điểm xuất phát.

sections.heading: Sự tương phản trong một cặp
sections.explanation: "집에 있어요" là một trạng thái — tôi ở nhà. "집에서 일해요" là một hành động — tôi làm việc ở nhà. Hỏi bản thân xem liệu có gì được làm thực tế ở đó không.

quiz: Câu "Tôi học tập ở trường" dùng hạt từ nào sau 학교?
Câu nào đúng cho "Tôi đi đến trường"?
에서 có nghĩa gì ngoài "ở"?

ja.title: 존댓말の基本
ja.summary: 韓国語はすべての文に敬語レベルを選びます。요から始め、습니다をいつ使うかを知っています。

sections.heading: あなたが会う3つのレベル
sections.explanation: 반말（カジュアル、요なし）は親友と子供向け。해요체（요で終わる）は丁寧で、ほぼすべての場所で安全です。합쇼체（습니다/ㅂ니다で終わる）は正式です—ニュース、プレゼンテーション、軍隊、カスタマーサービス。

sections.heading: 敬語시
sections.explanation: あなたが話している人に敬意を示すために（リスナーではなく）、動詞に으시/시を挿入します。自分について使用することは決してありません。

sections.heading: 自分のための謙虚な言葉
sections.explanation: 一部の単語には、丁寧な会社で自分について言及するときに使用する謙虚なバージョンがあります：나の代わりに저、내の代わりに제。

quiz: どの終わりが日常使用に対して丁寧で安全ですか？
動詞で시をいつ使いますか？
どの代名詞が「私」の丁寧な言葉ですか？

zh.title: 존댓말基础
zh.summary: 韩语为每个句子选择一个礼貌程度。从요开始，知道什么时候用습니다。

sections.heading: 你会遇到的三个级别
sections.explanation: 반말（随意，没有요）用于亲密朋友和孩子。해요체（以요结尾）是礼貌的，几乎到处都安全。합쇼체（以습니다/ㅂ니다结尾）是正式的——新闻、演讲、军队、客服。

sections.heading: 敬语시
sections.explanation: 为了对你谈论的人表示尊重（不是听众），在动词中插入으시/시。绝不要用于自己。

sections.heading: 对自己的谦虚词
sections.explanation: 某些词有你在礼貌场合用于自己时的谦虚版本：저代替나，제代替내。

quiz: 哪个结尾既礼貌又对日常使用安全？
你什么时候在动词中使用시？
哪个代词是"我"的礼貌词？

vi.title: 존댓말 cơ bản
vi.summary: Tiếng Hàn chọn mức độ lịch sự cho mỗi câu. Bắt đầu với 요, và biết khi nào dùng 습니다.

sections.heading: Ba cấp độ bạn sẽ gặp
sections.explanation: 반말 (tự nhiên, không có 요) dành cho bạn thân và trẻ em. 해요체 (kết thúc bằng 요) là lịch sự và an toàn ở hầu hết nơi. 합쇼체 (kết thúc bằng 습니다/ㅂ니다) là chính thức — tin tức, thuyết trình, quân đội, dịch vụ khách hàng.

sections.heading: Tôn kính 시
sections.explanation: Để thể hiện tôn trọng với người bạn đang nói về (không phải người nghe), chèn 으시/시 vào động từ. Không bao giờ dùng nó về bản thân.

sections.heading: Từ khiêm tốn cho bản thân
sections.explanation: Một số từ có phiên bản khiêm tốn mà bạn dùng khi nói về bản thân trong môi trường lịch sự: 저 thay vì 나, 제 thay vì 내.

quiz: Kết thúc nào vừa lịch sự vừa an toàn cho cách dùng hàng ngày?
Bạn khi nào dùng 시 trong động từ?
Đại từ nào là từ lịch sự cho "tôi"?

ja.title: 数と数え言葉
ja.summary: 韓国語には2つの数体系があり、物を数えるには数え言葉が必要です。

sections.heading: 2つのシステム
sections.explanation: ネイティブ韓国語番号（하나、둘、셋…）は物、人、時間を数えます。シノ-韓国語番号（일、이、삼…）はお金、日付、分、電話番号、および99以上のものを処理します。

sections.heading: 数え言葉
sections.explanation: あなたは「2匹の猫」と言うことはできません。パターンは名詞 + 数字 + 数え言葉です：개は物体用、명は人用、마리は動物用、잔はカップ用、병はボトル用。

sections.heading: フォームを変更する4つ
sections.explanation: 数え言葉の前に、하나/둘/셋/넷は한/두/세/네に短縮されます。스물は스무になります。他は形式を保ちます。

quiz: お金にはどの数字システムを使いますか？
「2杯のコーヒー」とどう言いますか？
「두시삼십분」で、時間と分が異なるシステムなのはなぜですか？

zh.title: 数字和量词
zh.summary: 韩语有两个数字系统，计数东西需要量词。

sections.heading: 两个系统
sections.explanation: 本地韩语数字（하나、둘、셋…）计算东西、人和小时。汉字数字（일、이、삼…）处理金钱、日期、分钟、电话号码和任何大于99的数字。

sections.heading: 量词
sections.explanation: 你不能只说"两只猫"。模式是名词 + 数字 + 量词：个表示对象，명表示人，마리表示动物，잔表示杯子，병表示瓶子。

sections.heading: 改变形状的四个
sections.explanation: 在量词前，하나/둘/셋/넷缩为한/두/세/네。스물变成스무。其他的保持形式。

quiz: 你用哪个数字系统表示金钱？
你怎么说"两杯咖啡"？
在"두시삼십분"中，为什么小时和分钟是不同系统？

vi.title: Số và từ đếm
vi.summary: Tiếng Hàn có hai hệ thống số, và đếm thứ cần một từ đếm.

sections.heading: Hai hệ thống
sections.explanation: Số tiếng Hàn bản địa (하나, 둘, 셋…) đếm thứ, người và giờ. Số Hán-Hàn (일, 이, 삼…) xử lý tiền bạc, ngày tháng, phút, số điện thoại và bất kỳ số nào trên 99.

sections.heading: Từ đếm
sections.explanation: Bạn không thể chỉ nói "hai chú mèo". Mô thức là danh từ + số + từ đếm: 개 cho vật, 명 cho người, 마리 cho động vật, 잔 cho cốc, 병 cho chai.

sections.heading: Bốn cái thay đổi hình thức
sections.explanation: Trước một từ đếm, 하나/둘/셋/넷 rút ngắn thành 한/두/세/네. 스물 trở thành 스무. Cái khác giữ nguyên hình thức.

quiz: Bạn dùng hệ thống số nào cho tiền bạc?
Bạn nói "hai tách cà phê" như thế nào?
Trong "두시삼십분", tại sao giờ và phút là hệ thống khác nhau?

ja.title: Saying 'and' and 'with' (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three ways to link two nouns. The same words also mean 'with someone'. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Linking two nouns
sections.explanation: To join nouns, attach 하고 (neutral, very common in speech), 와/과 (a touch more formal and used in writing), or (이)랑 (casual). 와 follows a vowel, 과 follows a consonant; 이랑 follows a consonant, 랑 a vowel. 하고 never changes.

sections.heading: The same words mean 'with'
sections.explanation: Attach the same particle to a person and you get 'together with'. Adding 같이 or 함께 after it makes the 'together' part explicit.

sections.heading: Do not use these to link sentences
sections.explanation: 하고 and 와/과 only join nouns. To join two whole clauses you need the verb ending ~고. English 'and' covers both jobs, Korean keeps them separate.

quiz: Which particle links nouns and is the most neutral in everyday speech?
'책' ends in a consonant. Which form of 와/과 follows it?
How do you join two clauses, as in 'I eat and I drink'?

ja.title: 이 / 그 / 저 — this, that, that over there (Japanese)
ja.summary: Korean splits 'that' in two: 그 for near the listener or already mentioned, 저 for far from you both. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Three distances, not two
sections.explanation: 이 is near the speaker, 그 is near the listener or something you both already talked about, and 저 is far from both of you. English only has this and that, so 그 is the one that needs practice.

sections.heading: Standing alone: 이것 / 그것 / 저것
sections.explanation: 이/그/저 must sit in front of a noun. To say this one on its own, add 것 (thing). In speech these contract to 이거, 그거, 저거.

sections.heading: Places: 여기 / 거기 / 저기
sections.explanation: The same three-way split applies to places. 여기 is here, 거기 is there by you or the place we mentioned, 저기 is over there in sight of us both. 저기요 is also how you politely get a stranger's attention.

quiz: You want the book the listener is holding. Which word do you use?

ja.title: Future with ~(으)ㄹ 거예요 (Japanese)
ja.summary: The everyday future: plans, predictions and 'I'm going to'. Add ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel, 을 거예요 after a consonant. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Building the form
sections.explanation: Take the verb stem. If it ends in a vowel, attach ㄹ 거예요 directly to that syllable. If it ends in a consonant, attach 을 거예요. Stems ending in ㄹ just take 거예요.

sections.heading: Plans and intentions
sections.explanation: With a first-person subject this is your plan. It is the form you reach for when someone asks what you are doing this weekend.

sections.heading: Guesses about other people
sections.explanation: With a third-person subject the same form becomes a prediction: probably, I bet. Context tells you which reading is meant.

sections.heading: The near-future 아/어요 shortcut
sections.explanation: For something already fixed and imminent, plain 아/어요 with a time word is more natural than the full future form. Both are correct; the plain form sounds more settled.

quiz: What is the future form of 먹다?
Stems ending in a vowel take…
'그 영화는 재미있을 거예요' most likely means…

ja.title: Wanting things: ~고 싶다 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Attach 고 싶어요 to a verb stem for 'I want to…'. For other people you need 고 싶어하다. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Stem + 고 싶어요
sections.explanation: No vowel matching needed — 고 싶다 attaches straight to any verb stem. Conjugate 싶다 like a normal descriptive verb: 싶어요, 싶었어요, 싶을 거예요.

sections.heading: Other people want: 고 싶어하다
sections.explanation: Korean treats another person's desire as something you observe, not something you feel. So for he/she/they, switch to 고 싶어해요. Using plain 고 싶어요 about someone else sounds wrong.

sections.heading: Wanting a thing, not an action
sections.explanation: 고 싶다 needs a verb. To want a noun, use 갖고 싶다 (want to have) or 필요하다 (to need), which takes 이/가, not 을/를.

quiz: How do you say 'I want to eat'?
Which form describes what your friend wants?
Which particle does 필요하다 take?

ja.title: Ability: ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다 and 못 (Japanese)
ja.summary: ~(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 is 'can', ~(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 is 'cannot', and 못 is the quick spoken 'can't'. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Can and cannot
sections.explanation: 수 literally means a way or method. Stem + (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 is 'there is a way to do it' — you can. Swap 있어요 for 없어요 and you cannot. The (으) follows the same rule as the future form.

sections.heading: 못 — blocked by circumstance

sections.heading: Knowing how: ~(으)ㄹ 줄 알다

ja.title: Because: ~아/어서 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Join a reason to a result with 아/어서. It also means 'and then' for actions that follow on from each other. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Reason and result
sections.explanation: Conjugate the first verb into its 아/어 form and add 서. The reason clause never carries tense — put 았/었 or 겠 only on the final verb.

sections.heading: No commands or suggestions after it
sections.explanation: This is the one restriction to remember: you cannot follow 아/어서 with an order or a let's-do suggestion. For those you need ~(으)니까 instead.

sections.heading: The 'and then' use
sections.explanation: With action verbs, 아/어서 can also link two steps where the second depends on the first — you go somewhere and then do something there. Compare with plain ~고, which just lists unrelated steps.

ja.title: Asking politely: ~(으)세요 and ~아/어 주세요 (Japanese)
ja.summary: (으)세요 tells someone to do something politely; 아/어 주세요 asks them to do it for you. (Japanese)

sections.heading: (으)세요 — polite instruction
sections.explanation: This is the honorific 시 plus the polite ending. Add 세요 after a vowel stem and 으세요 after a consonant. It covers everything from please sit down to have a good day.

sections.heading: 아/어 주세요 — do it for me
sections.explanation: 주다 means to give. Attaching it after the 아/어 form adds the sense of doing the action as a favour to the speaker. This is what you use in shops, taxis and restaurants.

sections.heading: Softening and negative requests
sections.explanation: Slip 좀 in before the verb to soften any request — it literally means a little but works like please. For please don't, use 지 마세요.

ja.summary: Stem + 고 있어요 is the -ing form: an action happening right now or ongoing in your life. (Japanese)

ja.title: Linking clauses: ~고 and ~지만 (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~고 — and
sections.explanation: Attach 고 to the plain stem, with no vowel matching and no tense on the first clause. It lists things in order or simply piles up facts.

sections.heading: ~지만 — but

sections.heading: Starting a fresh sentence
sections.explanation: To begin a new sentence with and or but, use the standalone connectors 그리고 and 그렇지만 / 하지만. They do the same work between sentences that 고 and 지만 do inside one.

ja.title: ~(으)니까 vs ~아/어서 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Both mean 'because', but only 니까 can be followed by a command or a suggestion. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Building ~(으)니까
sections.explanation: Add 니까 to a vowel stem and 으니까 to a consonant stem. Unlike 아/어서, this one happily takes tense markers: 했으니까, 갔으니까.

sections.heading: The dividing line
sections.explanation: 아/어서 states an objective cause and cannot precede a command, a request or a let's-do form. 니까 gives the speaker's own reasoning and can precede all of them. When in doubt before an imperative, use 니까.

sections.heading: Where each one is fixed
sections.explanation: Apologies and thanks are the classic 아/어서 territory — 늦어서 죄송합니다 is set, and 늦으니까 죄송합니다 sounds like you are blaming the listener. Conversely, 니까 also introduces a discovery: I did X, and then I found out Y.

sections.heading: Give it a go

sections.heading: Questions, suggestions, commands

sections.heading: Give me: ~아/어 달라고

ja.title: Talking about frequency and degree (Japanese)
ja.summary: Korean prefers hedged claims. These patterns say 'rather', 'tend to' and 'about as much as'. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄴ / ~는 편이다 — tends to be
sections.explanation: Attach the modifier form plus 편이다 to say something falls on one side of a scale rather than being absolutely so. Direct assertions can sound blunt in Korean, so this is very common.

sections.heading: ~만큼 and ~보다 — comparisons
sections.explanation: 보다 marks what you compare against (than), and 만큼 marks an equal degree (as much as). 더 and 덜 add more and less. Note 보다 attaches to the standard, which is the reverse of English word order.

sections.heading: Frequency words
sections.explanation: 항상, 자주, 가끔, 별로, 전혀 sit before the verb. 별로 and 전혀 require a negative verb to follow — leaving the verb positive is ungrammatical.

ja.title: The irregular verb families (Japanese)
ja.summary: Six patterns cover nearly every irregular verb in Korean. Learn the family, not the word. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ㅂ and ㄷ irregulars
sections.explanation: ㅂ-irregulars turn ㅂ into 우 before a vowel ending: 춥다 becomes 추워요. ㄷ-irregulars turn ㄷ into ㄹ: 듣다 becomes 들어요. Both are regular before consonant endings.

sections.heading: ㅅ and 르 irregulars
sections.explanation: ㅅ-irregulars drop the ㅅ but keep the vowels apart: 낫다 becomes 나아요. 르-irregulars double the ㄹ and take 라/러: 모르다 becomes 몰라요, 부르다 becomes 불러요.

sections.heading: ㅡ, ㄹ and ㅎ
sections.explanation: The ㅡ vowel drops before 아/어: 바쁘다 becomes 바빠요, 예쁘다 becomes 예뻐요. Stems ending in ㄹ drop it before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ: 살다 becomes 삽니다, 사세요. ㅎ-irregular colour adjectives become ㅐ: 그렇다 becomes 그래요.

sections.heading: The look-alikes that are regular
sections.explanation: Not every stem ending in ㅂ or ㄷ is irregular. 좁다, 입다, 잡다 are regular ㅂ verbs; 받다, 닫다, 믿다 are regular ㄷ verbs. There is no rule — these have to be learned individually.

ja.title: Passive and causative basics (Japanese)
ja.summary: The infixes 이/히/리/기 make a verb passive; adding 우/구/추 to the set makes it causative. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Passive with 이/히/리/기
sections.explanation: One of four syllables slots into the stem to turn the object into the subject. Which one a verb takes is fixed by the verb, not by a rule, so learn them in pairs. The old object now takes 이/가.

sections.heading: Causative with 이/히/리/기/우/구/추
sections.explanation: The same infixes plus three more make someone do something. 먹다 becomes 먹이다 (to feed), 자다 becomes 재우다 (to put to sleep), 앉다 becomes 앉히다 (to seat).

sections.heading: The regular alternatives
sections.explanation: When a verb has no infix form, use 아/어지다 for the passive and 게 하다 for the causative. These work on almost any verb and are the safe fallback.

quiz: 보다 in its passive form is…
What does 먹이다 mean?

ja.title: Making verbs into nouns (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three ways to say 'the act of doing' — and they are not interchangeable. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~기 — the activity itself
sections.explanation: Attach 기 to a plain stem. It names an activity in the abstract and is what fixed patterns like 기 쉽다, 기 전에 and 기 때문에 are built from. It is also the form used in titles and instructions.

sections.heading: ~는 것 — the concrete instance
sections.explanation: 것 means thing, so 는 것 refers to the specific act or fact in question. In speech it contracts to 는 게 (subject) and 는 걸 (object). Use it when you can point at what you mean.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㅁ — the written noun
sections.explanation: The most formal of the three. It appears in dictionary entries, notices, memos and note-taking, where it states a fact compactly. Some ㅁ nouns have frozen into ordinary vocabulary: 웃음, 믿음, 죽음.

quiz: Which nominalizer appears in fixed patterns like ~기 전에 and ~기 쉽다?

ja.title: ~더니 and ~았/었더니 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Two cousins with a strict subject rule: 더니 reports what someone else did, 았/었더니 what you did. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~더니 — I observed, and then
sections.explanation: Attach 더니 to the stem to link something you personally witnessed with what followed. The subject must be someone other than the speaker, and you must have seen it yourself.

sections.heading: ~았/었더니 — I did, and then I found
sections.explanation: With the past marker in front, the subject flips to the speaker. You did something, and the second clause is the result or discovery. This is the form for I went there and found that…

sections.heading: Keeping it apart from ~니까
sections.explanation: 니까 gives a reason; 더니 reports a sequence you witnessed and often implies the second clause was a natural consequence. Swapping them is not ungrammatical but changes the flavour from because to and sure enough.

quiz: Who is the subject of a ~더니 clause?

ja.title: ~길래 — since it was like that, I… (Japanese)
ja.summary: A reason you noticed from outside, prompting your own spontaneous action. (Japanese)

sections.heading: How it works
sections.explanation: Attach 길래 to the stem. The first clause is an external circumstance you observed; the second is what you decided to do about it. The second clause subject is almost always the speaker.

sections.heading: Why not just 니까
sections.explanation: 니까 is neutral reasoning and works with any subject and any following sentence type. 길래 is narrower: an outside trigger plus your own past action. It cannot be followed by a command, a suggestion or a plain future plan.

sections.heading: In questions: what on earth
sections.explanation: In a question, 길래 asks what circumstance produced a surprising result. It carries a note of curiosity or mild reproach.

quiz: In a ~길래 sentence, who normally performs the action in the second clause?

ja.title: Blaming and crediting a cause (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three cause markers coloured by outcome: unintended, blamed, and thanked. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~는 바람에 — because of it, unintentionally
sections.explanation: Attach 는 바람에 to an action verb stem. The result is always unexpected and usually unwanted, and the whole sentence sits in the past. You cannot use it about something you planned.

sections.heading: ~탓에 / ~때문에 — fault and plain cause
sections.explanation: 때문에 is the neutral because of. 탓에 assigns blame and only fits bad outcomes. Both attach to nouns directly and to verbs via the modifier form: 는 탓에, 기 때문에.

sections.heading: ~덕분에 — thanks to
sections.explanation: The mirror image of 탓에: it credits a good outcome. Note that 때문에 cannot start a sentence on its own — use 그렇기 때문에 for that.

quiz: What kind of result does ~는 바람에 always describe?

ja.title: The written plain style ~ㄴ/는다 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Books, essays, newspapers and diaries drop the 요 entirely and use the neutral 한다 form. (Japanese)

sections.heading: The four endings
sections.explanation: Action verbs take ㄴ다 after a vowel and 는다 after a consonant. Descriptive verbs and 있다/없다 take plain 다. Nouns take (이)다. Past is 았/었다 for everything, future (으)ㄹ 것이다.

sections.heading: It is a register, not rudeness
sections.explanation: This style has no listener built into it, so it is neither polite nor impolite — it simply addresses no one. That is why it suits printed text. Spoken to a person's face, though, it lands as blunt 반말.

sections.heading: Other things that change in writing
sections.explanation: Written Korean also prefers 나 over 저, drops most sentence-final particles like 요 and 네, replaces 그래서 with 따라서 or 그러므로, and favours Sino-Korean vocabulary over native equivalents.

quiz: How does the action verb 마시다 appear in written plain style?
Descriptive verbs like 춥다 in this style are written…

zh.title: The written plain style ~ㄴ/는다 (Chinese)

sections.heading: The four endings
sections.explanation: Action verbs take ㄴ다 after a vowel and 는다 after a consonant. Descriptive verbs and 있다/없다 take plain 다. Nouns take (이)다. Past is 았/었다 for everything, future (으)ㄹ 것이다.

sections.heading: It is a register, not rudeness
sections.explanation: This style has no listener built into it, so it is neither polite nor impolite — it simply addresses no one. That is why it suits printed text. Spoken to a person's face, though, it lands as blunt 반말.

sections.heading: Other things that change in writing
sections.explanation: Written Korean also prefers 나 over 저, drops most sentence-final particles like 요 and 네, replaces 그래서 with 따라서 or 그러므로, and favours Sino-Korean vocabulary over native equivalents.

ja.title: Contracted quotations: ~대요, ~냬요, ~재요, ~래요 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Spoken Korean squeezes 다고 해요 down to 대요. Four endings, one for each sentence type. (Japanese)

sections.heading: The four contractions
sections.explanation: 다고 해요 becomes 대요, 냐고 해요 becomes 냬요, 자고 해요 becomes 재요, and (으)라고 해요 becomes (으)래요. These dominate casual speech — the full forms sound stiff in conversation.

sections.heading: Hearsay you did not witness
sections.explanation: 대요 also works with no named source, meaning it is said that or apparently. This is how you pass on weather forecasts, gossip and things you read.

sections.heading: Do not confuse it with ~ㄴ대요 as surprise
sections.explanation: Nouns quote as (이)래요, not 대요: 학생이래요. Also, a rising 대요 at the end of your own question turns it into an expression of disbelief. Tone carries a lot here.

ja.title: As soon as: ~자마자 and ~는 대로 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Both mean 'the moment X happens', but only one of them can point at the future. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~자마자 — immediately after
sections.explanation: Attach 자마자 to the plain stem. It works for past and future alike and simply reports that two events touched. No tense goes on the first clause.

sections.heading: ~는 대로 — as soon as, for things still to come
sections.explanation: Attach 는 대로 to an action verb. It carries a sense of intention, so it points forward and cannot describe a past accident. It is the standard form for making commitments.

sections.heading: 대로's other meaning: exactly as
sections.explanation: After a past modifier or a noun, 대로 means in accordance with. 말한 대로 is as I said; 계획대로 is according to plan. Same word, quite different job.

quiz: Which form cannot be used for an unintended past event?

ja.title: Recalling with ~더라고요 and ~던 (Japanese)
ja.summary: The 더 marker replays something you personally experienced and are now reporting back. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~더라고요 — I saw it myself
sections.explanation: Attach 더라고요 to the stem to report a discovery you made in person. The rule is strict: you must have witnessed it, and the subject is normally not you, because you do not observe yourself from outside.

sections.heading: ~던 — the modifier of memory
sections.explanation: 던 in front of a noun marks something recalled: ongoing back then, repeated back then, or left unfinished. 았/었던 marks a completed past you are now recalling as distant.

sections.heading: Also ~더라 and ~던데요
sections.explanation: The casual version is 더라. Combined with 는데 you get 던데요, which reports an observation while inviting the listener to respond to it.

quiz: What does the 더 marker require?

ja.title: Purpose: ~(으)려고, ~기 위해, ~고자 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three ways to say 'in order to', separated by formality and by what kind of goal is involved. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~(으)려고 — personal intention
sections.explanation: The everyday one. The subject of both clauses must be the same person, and the second clause cannot be a command or a suggestion. On its own, (으)려고 하다 means to be about to or to intend to.

sections.heading: ~기 위해(서) — for the sake of
sections.explanation: More formal and more goal-oriented, common in writing and speeches. Unlike (으)려고, it can be followed by a command. After a noun, use 을/를 위해.

sections.heading: ~고자 and ~(으)러
sections.explanation: 고자 is the most formal of the set and belongs to written and ceremonial language. (으)러 is different again: it only attaches to a goal that is followed by a verb of movement — going or coming somewhere to do something.

ja.title: Even if: ~아/어도 and ~더라도 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Concessive clauses that grant the point and then push past it, ordered from everyday to literary. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~아/어도 — even if, even though
sections.explanation: Take the 아/어 form and add 도. It covers both a real concession (even though it is so) and a hypothetical one (even if it were). Tense goes on the final verb.

sections.heading: ~더라도 — even supposing
sections.explanation: Stronger and more hypothetical than 아/어도. It concedes something you consider unlikely or extreme, and often pairs with 아무리 or 설령.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ지라도 and ~(으)ㄴ들
sections.explanation: These belong to formal writing and rhetoric. (으)ㄹ지라도 is a heightened even though; (으)ㄴ들 is a rhetorical even if, usually implying it would make no difference.

quiz: Which is the everyday 'even if'?

ja.title: Degree and proportion (Japanese)
ja.summary: Patterns for saying how much, to what extent, and the more X the more Y. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 정도로 — to the extent that
sections.explanation: Put a vivid comparison in the first clause and 정도로 turns it into a measure of the second. English usually renders it as so much that.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 만큼 — as much as
sections.explanation: Close to 정도로 but focused on matching a quantity rather than illustrating an extreme. 만큼 also attaches straight to nouns for as much as X.

sections.explanation: Repeat the same verb in both slots: conditional 면 first, then (으)ㄹ수록. In speech the first half is often dropped, leaving just (으)ㄹ수록.

ja.title: Stating general truths (Japanese)
ja.summary: Endings that frame something as inevitable, natural, or the way of the world. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~기 마련이다 — it is bound to happen
sections.explanation: Attach 기 마련이다 to a stem to say that the outcome is only natural given how things are. It carries a resigned, worldly tone and appears constantly in proverbs and advice. 게 마련이다 is an equally correct variant.

sections.heading: ~는 법이다 — that is how it works
sections.explanation: 법 means law or way. This ending asserts a principle rather than a tendency, so it sounds more didactic than 기 마련이다. It is what an elder says when delivering a life lesson.

sections.heading: Neighbouring patterns
sections.explanation: ~는 셈이다 says it amounts to; ~기 십상이다 warns that something bad is likely; ~는 경향이 있다 states a tendency more neutrally and belongs to written or academic register.

quiz: Which ending frames the result as only natural and slightly resigned?
'거의 다 끝난 셈이에요' means…

ja.title: Not only that: ~(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (Japanese)
ja.summary: 뿐 means 'only'. Negate it and you get 'not only' — the workhorse of formal addition. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 — not only… but also
sections.explanation: Attach the (으)ㄹ modifier plus 뿐만 아니라 to a verb, or 뿐만 아니라 directly to a noun. The second clause usually carries 도. It is the standard connector for building a case in writing.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 — nothing more than
sections.explanation: Left positive, 뿐이다 restricts: that and nothing else. It often carries a note of modesty or of dismissal, depending on what you attach it to.

sections.heading: The same job, other registers
sections.explanation: In speech, 도 ~고 or 게다가 does the adding. In formal writing you will also meet ~(으)ㅁ은 물론이고 and ~기도 하다. Choosing among them is mostly a register decision, not a meaning one.

sections.heading: ~적 (的) — the -ic / -al suffix

ja.title: Sentence endings that carry attitude (Japanese)
ja.summary: These endings add nothing to the facts and everything to the relationship between speaker and listener. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~잖아요 — you know this already
sections.explanation: Use it to remind the listener of shared knowledge. It can sound warm and collaborative, or impatient, depending entirely on tone — which is why learners are often warned off it with strangers.

sections.heading: ~거든요 — here's the background
sections.explanation: It supplies a reason the listener does not yet have, often setting up what you are about to say. Ending a first sentence on 거든요 signals that more is coming.

sections.heading: ~네요 and ~군요 — fresh realisation
sections.explanation: Both mark something you have just noticed. 네요 is the everyday spoken one and sounds mildly impressed; 군요 (or 구나 casually) is a touch more bookish and reads as ah, I see.

sections.heading: ~지요 / ~죠 — seeking agreement
sections.explanation: 지요 assumes the listener agrees, like an English tag question. It also softens a suggestion or an offer, and in the first person it signals willing acceptance.

ja.title: Conjecture: ~(으)ㄹ 텐데, ~(으)ㄹ 테니까, ~(으)ㄹ 걸 (Japanese)
ja.summary: Speculation with consequences — guessing, and then acting on the guess. (Japanese)

sections.explanation: 터 is a bound noun meaning expectation. 텐데 states a supposition and leaves a concern or a contrast hanging. Trailing off on 텐데요 is a common way to voice worry politely.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 테니까 — since I expect, you should
sections.explanation: The same 터 plus 니까. The first clause is your prediction or your own intention; the second tells the listener what follows from it. This is the natural way to offer to handle something.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 걸(요) and ~(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬다
sections.explanation: (으)ㄹ 걸요 is a soft guess: probably, I'd say. But past 았/었을 걸 그랬다 is entirely different — it is regret about a road not taken.

quiz: Which form offers to handle something on the listener's behalf?

ja.title: Connectives for formal prose (Japanese)
ja.summary: The connectors that make writing read as an argument rather than a conversation. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Contrast: ~(으)ㄴ/는 반면(에)
sections.explanation: 반면 means the opposite side. It sets two facts against each other in a balanced way, unlike 지만 which simply turns. Written Korean strongly prefers it for structured comparison.

sections.heading: Concession: ~(으)ㅁ에도 불구하고
sections.explanation: The formal despite. It attaches to the ㅁ nominalizer, or straight to a noun with 에도 불구하고. Reserve it for writing; in speech it sounds like a press release.

sections.heading: Cause: ~(으)로 인해 and ~에 따라
sections.explanation: (으)로 인해 is the formal owing to, used where speech would use 때문에. 에 따라 means in accordance with or depending on, and marks a variable the outcome tracks.

quiz: Which connective sets two facts against each other in balanced contrast?

ja.title: Regret, hindsight and no choice (Japanese)
ja.summary: Looking back at what should have happened, and forward at what cannot be avoided. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~았/었어야 했다 — should have
sections.explanation: Put the verb in the past, add 어야, then 했다 or 하는데. It states an unmet obligation. The 했는데 variant softens it into a lingering regret rather than a verdict.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 — no choice but
sections.explanation: 밖에 means outside of, and it always demands a negative verb. Literally there is nothing outside of doing it, so: I have no option. It can also describe an inevitable outcome rather than a decision.

sections.heading: ~(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 and ~고 말았다
sections.explanation: (으)ㄹ 뻔했다 is a near miss: it almost happened but did not. 고 말았다 is the opposite — it ended up happening, usually to the speaker's dismay.

ja.title: Framing a claim carefully (Japanese)
ja.summary: Advanced Korean rarely asserts flatly. These patterns restate, qualify and estimate. (Japanese)

ja.title: Reading the news (Japanese)
ja.summary: Headlines drop particles and tense; body text runs on a small set of reporting verbs. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Headline compression
sections.explanation: Korean headlines strip particles, use the bare noun or the ㄴ/는다 form, and mark the future with a bare stem plus 할 듯 or 전망. A dash or comma often stands in for the topic particle.

sections.heading: The reporting verbs
sections.explanation: Body text cycles through a small set: 밝혔다 (stated), 전했다 (reported), 덧붙였다 (added), 지적했다 (pointed out), 강조했다 (emphasised). Learning them makes any article far easier to skim.

ja.summary: Nominal density, impersonal framing, and the connectors that hold an argument together. (Japanese)

ja.title: The full range of speech levels (Japanese)
ja.summary: Beyond 반말 and 존댓말: six traditional levels, and where you still meet each one. (Japanese)

sections.heading: The six levels
sections.explanation: 하십시오체 (highest formal), 해요체 (polite informal), 하오체 and 하게체 (older middle levels), 해체 and 해라체 (casual and plain). Only 하십시오체, 해요체, 해체 and 해라체 are fully alive today.

sections.heading: Where the old levels survive
sections.explanation: 하오체 lingers in period dramas, public signs (출입을 금하오) and translated literature. 하게체 belongs to professors addressing students and older men addressing younger adult men. Reading them is a comprehension skill more than a production one.

sections.heading: Switching mid-conversation
sections.explanation: Koreans move between levels within one conversation to signal warmth, distance, irritation or a shift into private register. An abrupt drop into 반말 with a stranger is an act of aggression; a shift up into 하십시오체 with a friend reads as sarcasm or sudden formality.

ja.title: The full honorific system (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three axes — subject, object and listener — plus a vocabulary of humble and elevated words. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Three separate honorifics
sections.explanation: 주체 높임 elevates the sentence subject (시, 께서, 님). 객체 높임 elevates the object or recipient (께, 드리다, 뵙다, 여쭙다). 상대 높임 is the speech level aimed at the listener. All three can operate in one sentence independently.

sections.heading: Suppletive vocabulary
sections.explanation: Some words swap entirely rather than take 시: 먹다 becomes 드시다 or 잡수시다, 자다 becomes 주무시다, 있다 becomes 계시다, 말하다 becomes 말씀하시다, 죽다 becomes 돌아가시다. Nouns change too: 밥 becomes 진지, 나이 becomes 연세, 집 becomes 댁.

sections.heading: 압존법 and its decline
sections.explanation: Traditionally you lowered a middle-ranking person when speaking to someone senior to them — telling your grandfather that 아버지가 왔습니다, not 오셨습니다. Modern usage, and the National Institute of Korean Language, now accepts the honorific in most family and workplace settings. Learners should recognise 압존법 but need not apply it.

sections.heading: The over-honorific error
sections.explanation: Service Korean has spread 시 onto inanimate objects: 커피 나오셨습니다. This 사물 존대 is widely criticised as incorrect, though you will hear it constantly in cafes and shops. Recognise it; do not copy it.

ja.title: Distinguishing the cause markers (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three formal markers English collapses into 'by' or 'due to', but Korean keeps apart. (Japanese)

sections.heading: ~에 의해 — the agent
sections.explanation: Marks the doer in a passive sentence: who or what performed the action. It is the closest thing Korean has to the English by in a passive construction, and it belongs firmly to written register.

sections.heading: ~(으)로 인해 — the cause
sections.explanation: Marks a non-agentive cause: an event or condition that brought about a result. Swapping it for 에 의해 makes it sound as though the weather deliberately acted.

sections.heading: ~에 따라 — the variable
sections.explanation: Marks something the outcome tracks or conforms to: a rule, a standard, or a factor the result varies with. It is correlation and conformity, not causation.

sections.explanation: Marks the doer in a passive sentence: who or what performed the action. It is the closest thing Korean has to the English by in a passive construction, and it belongs firmly to written register.

sections.heading: ~(으)로 인해 — the cause
sections.explanation: Marks a non-agentive cause: an event or condition that brought about a result. Swapping it for 에 의해 makes it sound as though the weather deliberately acted.

sections.heading: ~에 따라 — the variable
sections.explanation: Marks something the outcome tracks or conforms to: a rule, a standard, or a factor the result varies with. It is correlation and conformity, not causation.

quiz: Which marker introduces the agent of a formal passive?
'상황에 따라 달라져요' expresses…

ja.title: Fine distinctions in causatives (Japanese)
ja.summary: Three ways to make someone do something, differing in directness and in who does the work. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Suffix causatives are direct
sections.explanation: The 이/히/리/기/우/구/추 forms usually describe the causer physically doing it: 먹이다 is spoon-feeding, 입히다 is dressing someone yourself. The causee is often not acting independently at all.

sections.heading: ~게 하다 is indirect
sections.explanation: The causee performs the action; you brought it about by instruction or permission. Depending on context it can be make, let or have someone do something.

sections.heading: ~시키다 — Sino-Korean nouns only
sections.explanation: 시키다 attaches to a Sino-Korean action noun, making the 하다 verb causative: 공부하다 becomes 공부시키다. It also means to order food. Attaching it to a native verb stem is ungrammatical.

quiz: '아이에게 옷을 입혔어요' implies…
What can 시키다 attach to?
Which causative can also mean 'let'?

ja.title: Literary and archaic forms (Japanese)
ja.summary: Endings you will read in poetry, scripture and historical drama but should not produce in conversation. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Elevated declaratives
sections.explanation: ~노라 (a solemn first-person declaration), ~도다 and ~로다 (exclamatory), ~리라 (a vow or prophecy about the future). These belong to poetry, anthems and translated classics.

sections.heading: Archaic connectors
sections.explanation: ~느니 (rather than), ~거늘 (whereas, yet), ~건대 (as for, if I may say). You meet them in proverbs and formal address more than anywhere else.

sections.heading: Reading old spelling
sections.explanation: Pre-1988 texts use spellings that no longer match the standard: 읍니다 for 습니다, 어떻읍니까 for 어떻습니까, and the obsolete letter ㆍ in very old texts. Historical dramas also revive 하오체 and 하게체 wholesale.

quiz: Where would you expect to meet ~노라?

ja.title: 구어체 vs 문어체 (Japanese)
ja.summary: The systematic differences that make writing sound like writing and speech sound like speech. (Japanese)

sections.heading: Contractions and dropped particles
sections.explanation: Speech contracts relentlessly — 이것은 to 이건, 나는 to 난, 무엇을 to 뭘 — and drops 을/를 and 이/가 whenever context allows. Writing restores all of them.

sections.heading: Different vocabulary for the same idea
sections.explanation: Native words dominate speech and Sino-Korean words dominate writing. 그래서 becomes 따라서, 하지만 becomes 그러나, 아주 becomes 매우, 되게 becomes 상당히.

sections.heading: Filler, hedging and sentence length
sections.explanation: Speech is full of 좀, 뭐, 그냥, 약간 and trailing 는데요; writing removes them entirely and packs the content into longer, nominalised sentences. A common advanced error is writing exactly as one speaks, which reads as unserious.

quiz: In writing, 그래서 is typically replaced by…
What happens to 을/를 and 이/가 in casual speech?
Which of these belongs to written register?
